inline.s: Venerable Aniruddha, in a former life, had been a thief. One night he slipped into a temple to steal. Seeing the Buddha-lamp about to gutter out, he drew his arrow and used it to lift the wick; at once the lamp burst into brilliant, dazzling light. Aniruddha was seized with dread, and on the spot renounced evil for good. The evil karma he had wrought gradually dissolved, and the good he practiced gradually was perfected, until at last he attained the fruit of a sage.

Yang Zhonghe of the Song dynasty had served as the judicial assessor of Xuzhou. In the Tiansheng reign he was dispatched by the court to take up the post of judge in Caizhou. Because he had convicted men unjustly, the Northern Dipper memorialized against him, and grave punishment was about to fall. Overwhelmed with remorse and fear, Zhonghe at once resigned his post in Caizhou and vowed to cultivate a hundred good deeds to atone for his fault. Every time he met traveling monks or Daoists, the poor, the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, or households stricken by death or sickness, he never failed to give alms and relief. Within a few years he had given away his entire estate. Morning and evening he served the incense of the Perfected Lord Zhenwu with all his heart. Moved by his courage in reforming and pitying his straitened circumstances, the Perfected Lord transformed himself into a Daoist and entrusted him with the sacred lots of the Twelve Perfected Ones, so that he might earn a modest living, settle his life, and continue his cultivation. After his death he was received by the Great Emperor of Mount Tai and appointed to the spirit office of Registrar of Records at Maxi, and the court posthumously honored him as the Perfected Man Wuben.

Mr. Mao Qizong of the Ming dynasty said: “The six yao lines of the Qian hexagram in the Book of Changes conclude in auspiciousness. At the outset it speaks of no calamity; later, from self-complacency, come error and regret. Yet because at the end one can repent, one is thereby able to repair one’s faults and move toward the auspicious.”

Again Mr. Chen Liangmo said: “The poverty or wealth, rank or lowliness, long life or short life of a person — even his every sip and morsel, every act and rest — are all fixed by fate and cannot be resisted. Yet the pivot by which fortune and misfortune are turned lies in the individual himself, and ‘fate’ cannot confine him. For the fixed decree is Heaven’s appointment, while response is Heaven’s heart. Heaven takes the benefit of all things as its fundamental purpose; it is utterly sincere and free from the slightest partiality. If a person can from his inmost heart give rise to a single thought of saving others and benefiting things, and at the very outset acts with no ulterior motive, then though it be but an instant and a single small matter, because his inner sincerity reaches its utmost, it naturally ascends to move the heart of Heaven, like an echo answering a sound. This is the certain principle. Fate is the decree of Heaven; once the heart of Heaven is moved, the decree of Heaven turns in accordance with it — how could it possibly be confined? Consider the state’s system of punishment and reward, which surely cannot be altered at will. If a minister is truly able to move his sovereign’s heart with loyalty, then though he be banished or exiled, he may yet be recalled; at the very moment of execution the sovereign may issue a special pardon. In the briefest space, joy and anger change entirely — and what then is unalterable? From this one knows that the heart of Heaven and the decree of Heaven rise and fall together, and that the many deeds of hidden virtue and reward recorded through the ages are indeed clearly credible.”

Therefore the auspicious man, whose speech is good, whose sight is good, whose deeds are good — having three good deeds in a single day, at the end of three years Heaven will surely send him blessing. The inauspicious man, whose speech is evil, whose sight is evil, whose deeds are evil — having three evil deeds in a single day, at the end of three years Heaven will surely send him calamity. Why not strive to practice them!

Thus the auspicious man who strives to practice all good — because his speech is good, his sight is good, and his deeds are good — performs three good deeds in a single day; when the three years are fulfilled his good deeds are complete, and Heaven will surely grant him blessing and increase his years. As for the inauspicious man who constantly does evil — because his speech is evil, his sight is evil, and his deeds are evil — he commits three evil deeds in a single day; when the three years are fulfilled and his evil has reached the brim and overflowed, Heaven will surely bring calamity upon him and cut short his life. Therefore why should a man not strive to practice all good, so as to turn calamity into blessing?

This section sums up the whole text, and is the very path by which the teaching earnestly instructs men to do good and abandon evil. The word “therefore” here links what precedes and what follows. The “auspicious man” is the good man; because he practices good he obtains blessing, and so he is called auspicious. The “inauspicious man” is the evil man; because he practices evil he is about to meet misfortune, and so he is called inauspicious. As for the many evils and the many goods, they are too numerous to enumerate; in general they point to these three — good speech, good sight, and good deeds — which are precisely where we must truly set our hands to work. Good speech, for example, is not speaking what is contrary to propriety, rejoicing in recounting others’ goodness, urging men to do good, and so on. Good sight, for example, is not looking at what is contrary to propriety, delighting to see good men, loving to read good books, often noticing one’s own faults rather than others’ misdeeds. Good deeds, for example, is not acting contrary to propriety, never doing what is unlawful, boldly practicing goodness, ever adapting to circumstances for others’ convenience, accumulating all manner of hidden merit, guiding and leading within one’s region and extending to the four quarters, so that one transforms the world and leads all to do good together. Evil is precisely the opposite. Three years are a thousand days, the time of completion, for by then the good has accumulated and the evil has brimmed over.

The human mind is extremely agile and never constant. If a man’s mind has not changed over so long a time as three years, then the good or evil he has wrought has reached maturity. Here the word “Heaven” is pointed out because Heaven is the great sovereign that rewards good, punishes evil, grants blessing, and sends calamity — the very key and essence of the entire text. And this Heaven of which it speaks is our own mind. Mencius said: “To preserve one’s clear, intelligent mind and to nurture one’s Heaven-given nature — this is the way to serve and obey Heaven.”

The two words “surely” here do not assert it of the vast, dark, soundless, odorless Heaven, but of the good and evil in speech, sight, and deed that my heart has put forth over three years. What is called “all things are sought and obtained by oneself” is this very principle. The wise man delights in the Way and turns to it, not originally seeking blessing. If one does good only in order to seek blessing, then the heart has already sunk into self-interest. Therefore one ought only to do one’s utmost in oneself and accept Heaven’s rule, without the slightest hope, expectation, or eagerness. Yet the retribution of fortune and misfortune is induced by the good and evil of one’s own mind, and Heaven’s law must repay cause and effect. So the principle of fortune-and-misfortune recompense exists and pervades between heaven and earth, never missing by a hair. Those who regard doing good and removing evil as a matter belonging to their own duty are indeed of the highest and sharpest faculties. But the common people of the world are many — how could all be of the topmost capability? So those who, fearing calamity and seeking blessing, are willing to abandon evil and do good — these too are what the Supreme Old Lord hopes to transform, for He only fears that men will not seek blessing. And Mencius’s saying, “To seek it in the proper way and obtain it as decreed — in such seeking there is benefit in the obtaining,” is quite correct. If one seeks in the manner Mencius directs, naturally no harm will arise.

What is called “sending blessing” includes, for example, personally enjoying rank and emolument, having virtuous descendants, a prosperous household, prolonged years, and all matters going smoothly; even becoming a sage or worthy, an immortal or a Buddha, thoroughly awakening to one’s own nature, directly realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, delivering people and things, and establishing the supreme standard for ten thousand generations — all these are “sending blessing.”

What is called “sending calamity” includes, for example, personally suffering great misfortune, having wicked and perilous descendants who decline and perish; or a short life, a ruined household, and encountering setbacks in everything; even after death falling into the incessant hell, or transmigrating and being reborn among the brute creatures, suffering bitter torment for con after con, with evil karma extending to the descendants, condemned and reviled by the world for ten thousand years.

Alas! Judged by this, the way of fortune and misfortune is indeed vast! How inconceivable it is! The final line lays bare “strive to practice,” and this is only spoken with regard to the practice of all good — the master key of the entire text. The word “strive” is the most important method for moving toward good and correcting faults, while “practice” means to carry it out bodily. So “strive to practice” means to spur oneself and exert oneself, never retreating even at the cost of one’s life. The Book of History says: “The difficulty is not in knowing but in doing.” A common saying also goes: “Speaking a foot is not worth practicing an inch.” If one knows but does not act, one assuredly gains no benefit; and since one gains none, one cannot but sink into the great sea of birth and death to reap what one has sown. Therefore if men of the world wish to find the path of life, they must expend the effort of death. Master Zhu said: “When the vital yang-force arises, even metal and stone are pierced through; where the spirit arrives, what undertaking does not succeed!” If a man can be like this, he will surely reach the realm of perfect accomplishment, fulfilled merit, realized truth, or the attainment of the fruit of sagehood.

You must know that without practicing good there is no blessing, and without doing evil there is no calamity. This is the eternal, unchanging truth of the heavenly Way. Yet the retribution of good and evil is sometimes repaid upon the person himself, sometimes upon his descendants. Sometimes a man is an evil man in this life, but the good karmic conditions he planted in past lives have matured, so that though he should suffer calamity in this life, he instead receives blessing. Sometimes a man is a good man in this life, but the sins he committed in past lives have matured, so that though he should receive blessing in this life, he instead meets calamity. Only after the fortune and misfortune of former lives have been exhausted do the retributions of the good and evil done in this life come to be repaid one by one. This is merely a question of earlier or later — it is not that the retribution of good and evil has erred. Therefore it is said: “The visible laws of the court are swift yet may be fled; the hidden laws of the dead are slow yet never missed. The visible net of the law is loose and easily slipped through; the hidden net of the dead is dense and hard to escape.”

People of today, having done a single good deed by chance, at once wish to receive its reward; at the slightest disappointment they say, “The Way of Heaven is hard to know.” How could they understand that as long as a man is neither hungry nor cold, free of disaster and harm, a scholar has books to read, a farmer has fields to till, a craftsman has work to do, a merchant has business to trade, ever smiling and seldom frowning — are these not blessings of peace and safety? If it were otherwise, men’s wishes would never be exhausted and the world would be full of defects — how could everyone be rich, noble, and prosperous? Let the world only revere and trust the principle of the Tract of Response and Retribution, earnestly pursue it in every matter, and naturally blessing and emolument will be boundless and descendants honored and flourishing. Follow it for one year and ten thousand crimes are extinguished; four years and a hundred blessings arrive; seven years and descendants pass the examinations; ten years and life is prolonged; fifteen years and all things go as one wishes; twenty or thirty years and one is enrolled among the immortals; fifty years and the gods themselves revere him, and he takes his rank in the highest realm. These are the true, non-deceiving words of the Supreme Old Lord — only one fears that men of the world will not earnestly put them into practice.

Generally, one who fixes his mind on the Way, at the very moment he makes his vow, must save himself and save others, and self-deliverance and the deliverance of others require the dual cultivation of blessing and wisdom. Cultivating wisdom must lie in understanding the aim of practice and seeing one’s true nature; cultivating blessing must lie in observing the five human relationships and refining the mind amid the daily affairs of life. Moreover, the two must be coordinated and support one another. Thus God will await him with a heavenly decree, and the Buddhas will receive him into the Pure Land — not merely ascending beyond the highest realm, but in truth immediately realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, entering the state of non-arising and non-ceasing. Then he may enter the world to deliver sentient beings, thus completing this one great matter of fate. If one only hopes meagerly for long life and merely cultivates this life-force and nature, and if one fails to transcend birth and death, then when the blessing is exhausted one must still fall. Even one who is born in the highest heaven, the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought, whose lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand great kalpas (one great kalpa equals one billion three hundred forty-four million years), will in the end still fall and sink among the six destinies, never able to transcend the three realms. And the sentient beings caught in the six-fold transmigration are all so because they fail to awaken to their own wondrous bright mind; having gathered idle thoughts, they falsely induce the three realms (the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm), and amid these falsely sink with the seven destinies (the six destinies plus the realm of immortals are called the seven destinies); drawn and guided by karmic forces, each is born in a different path in accordance with the karma it has wrought. If one but thoroughly awakens the originally endowed nature of awareness, then one will understand that these false conditions were in the first place wholly nonexistent; and the power of his universally benefiting goodness can be upheld to completeness. For this reason, one can then conclude this great matter of fate, and it must be attributed to the dual cultivation of blessing and wisdom, attained to the state of consummation.

The Perfected Man Qiyun, Wang Zhi, in his Pan Shan Record of Sayings, speaks on good and evil. Someone asked how one could escape the karma of fortune and misfortune. The Master replied: “The karma of fortune and misfortune belongs to the shell of yin and yang; if you can get out of the shell of yin and yang, then there is no retribution of fortune or misfortune.” Then what is the shell of yin-yang good-and-evil? Whenever there is even a hair of selfish desire or self-interest in the mind, that belongs to the yin shell; whenever there is even a hair of a thought fond of doing good, that belongs to the yang shell. In yin there is evil retribution, in yang there is good retribution. If one can refine until the substance of the mind is empty and void, without good or evil, without the slightest obstruction, and can master oneself, then fortune and misfortune cannot bind him, cause and effect cannot entangle him — and such a one is a true man who has left the shell of yin and yang.

Master Zhu Xi of the Song dynasty, also known as Hui’an, held himself strictly to the rules and practiced them, which made later students feel quite inconvenient. How could they know that when neo-Confucianism was not yet thoroughly and clearly understood, if one lightly cast aside the rules, one could hardly enter the inner sanctum of the learning? Had Master Zhu not persisted in stemming the tide and propping up the sinking, the learning would long ago have collapsed and been lost. For at that time the fashion was to proscribe the Way-learning, classing it as false learning and denouncing it as heresy. Those who rose up in the clamor included Han Tuozhou’s troupe of players, Lin Lizhi’s attacks on dissent, and Wang Huai and Chen Jia’s nursing of grudges. The Six Classics and the teachings of Confucius and Mencius were a great prohibition of the age; the rectification of the mind and sincerity of the will were loathed and hated by those in power. Thus the upright gentlemen all held their breath and dared not act, while the fawning petty men all altered what they had learned and made themselves out to be masters of heterodox schools. Only Zhu Xi was able to carry the burden of the transmission of the Way alone, without worry or fear; in advancing and retreating he would not take a single step carelessly; subjected to slander he remained unyielding and at ease; in earnestly teaching his students, many worthy men came forth in succession; in discipline of himself, he never dared violate Yanzi’s four prohibitions. For this reason Confucian learning and neo-Confucianism rose like the sun at midday in that age — this was the effect of Zhu Xi’s vigorous practice.

Fan Yan of the Song dynasty was a man of Renhe. In the prime of life he passed the jinshi examination and served as a local official in commanderies and counties, rising later to the rank of senior minister. Every day he would reflect on how he might be loyal to his sovereign and how he might bring blessing to the people; in his words and actions he never dared to be careless. Even when alone in a hidden chamber where no one could see him, he preserved a vigilant, watchful, self-admonishing attitude. When his son grew up, he resigned his office and retired, clothed in coarse cloth and eating plain fare, no longer involving himself in worldly affairs, and quieting his mind to enter the Way. Every day he recited the great-vehicle scriptures such as the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra, and practiced their teachings. In spare moments he meditated and contemplated; not the slightest worldly matter touched him, and his own cultivation progressed naturally. By the Daguan reign he was in his nineties. Suddenly he awakened, and then instructed his attendants: “A person’s life in this world is like a play. When the drums and gongs sound, the various roles — leading man, leading lady, clown, and the rest — each perform their own artistry. But once the candle burns out and the lamp goes dark, what joy remains? Thus my coming into this world — in the twinkling of an eye it has been ninety years. It is truly like a dream’s illusion, swift as the morning dew and the lightning’s flash. Fortunately I have awakened to this Buddha-nature. This Buddha-nature has no boundary, no square or circle, no red, white, azure, or yellow, no long or short, above or below; no anger, no joy, no right, no wrong, no good, no evil. What is called being without a single thing yet containing all phenomena — this is the most true, most supreme truth of no coming and no going, wondrous beyond words. Its key lies only in whether a person can be sincere and diligent, one thought following the next, single-minded and unbroken. The Buddhas of the three times all emerge from this. This principle is precisely the truth the Diamond Sutra speaks of as real and not false; each of you should strive to practice it.” Having spoken, he sat in meditation and passed away. At once a strange fragrance filled the chamber, auspicious clouds spread across the sky, and manifold radiances illumined the world; these auspicious signs did not fade for several days. When the neighboring people heard of it, they came to gaze upon his auspicious passing.

The various cases of “strive to practice it” listed above are each instances of earnestly carrying out the principles of the three teachings — Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism — proceeding from basic learning to lofty attainment, all converging upon the exhaustive investigation of principle and the fulfillment of nature, and reaching the highest state of one’s true nature. These cases are recorded here as the finest models for practitioners of the three teachings; those who set their minds to learn should earnestly emulate them.

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said: “All undertakings grow from the small to the great.” Therefore all sentient beings endowed with blood and spirit can directly realize the supreme state of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Yet this supreme bodhi state is only reached by starting from the effort of being cautious with one’s own subtle thoughts — the practice of watchfulness in solitude — and extending it until it is complete. Did not Master Yuan Liaofan say: “What is past is like yesterday’s death; what is to come is like today’s birth.” So how could one be willing to abandon oneself, attribute all fortune and misfortune to Heaven’s appointment, and drift idly and carelessly through this life?

The world is vast in the extreme, and the myriad ages are distant in the extreme. Even if ten thousand hands and ten thousand eyes were used to rescue and help the world, they would still be insufficient. Therefore the most urgent thing is solely the education of people. And must one become a sage or worthy before one can teach? If a person truly rejoices at hearing good, delights at seeing good, and at all times and places speaks good words, discusses good deeds, tells of good retribution, and distributes good books, then the transformative instruction therein is already great. As for the subtle changes produced in the course of such teaching, their wonder is beyond what we ourselves can know. Moreover, teaching the common people is not as good as teaching the heroic. If one can obtain a hero and teach him, then he can produce the effect of turning heaven and earth around, carrying on the past and opening the future, and producing the function of layer upon layer of instruction — and then this teaching becomes exceedingly widespread and vast.

The transmission of the ancient sages, worthies, and canonical books through the ages is likewise this one great matter of fate. And this very text is the mysterious truth by which the Supreme Old Lord transforms the world, and the secret essential by which the Buddhas deliver sentient beings. Truly it is compassion carried to the utmost and wonder carried to the peak; it is certain to be transmitted forever and illumine heaven and earth. Whoever recites this text, practices this text, prints this text, or circulates this text also has in it a great matter of fate. Thus one can awaken this world, guide and transform the people, nourish the vital spirit of society, and create the welfare of humankind. Doing good together with others, heaven and earth are pure and serene; and the measure of the mind can contain the great void, ever full for myriad kalpas — truly inconceivable.
End of Volume Four, A Vernacular Abridgment of the Collected Annotations, Explanations, and Proof Cases of the Supreme Tract of Response and Retribution.
Encouraging Recitation Is the Root of Obtaining Blessing

At first the Tract of Response and Retribution was kept in the Daoist canon. Not until the Song emperor Zhenzong bestowed a million cash and commanded artisans to engrave it did it become widely known. At that time worthy scholars and gentlemen all strove to revere and uphold it. The Ming emperor Shizong also wrote a preface to it and published it to the realm. In the thirteenth year of the Shunzhi reign of the Qing dynasty, the emperor ordered the tract engraved and bestowed upon the ministers and extended to the literati. Such was the honor and practice shown to the tract across the dynasties. Yet it is not only treasured by humankind; the high heavens hold it in even greater reverence. For example, Wang Xun, when ill and wandering through the eastern mansion of the underworld, saw the characters of the Tract of Response and Retribution written in gold upon the hall, and the work was called the Golden Chapter. Yang Daoji, through illness, entered the underworld, and the netherworld office commanded him to urge the world widely to study and recite the tract. Zhou Chi was likewise admonished by the netherworld office: “After you return to life, you should spread this scripture far and wide. Those able to uphold it will not only escape the suffering of flood, fire, thieves, and illness; to seek offspring, long life, wealth, rank, or immortality, all are within this scripture.” Yet the sea of the mortal world is bitter affliction, and sentient beings are as if drunk, as if dreaming. The young and bold cling to their delusion and refuse to believe; when age has come and habits are formed, it is even harder to hope for their reform. Thus they live drunkenly, die dreaming, and cast away this life lightly.

Alas! Read the Tract of Response and Retribution and one awakens from drunkenness; read it and one wakes from dreaming. Not only can it turn calamity into blessing — it can truly raise the dead to life. Now I urge the world: first, to give rise to the mind of faith; second, to give rise to the mind of humility. Possessing these two minds, one may then read the tract. Every day burn incense and recite it once reverently; once one becomes familiar with it, there will be joy. All the more should one recite one line and study one line, recite one line and amend one line, and turn it over and over in careful reading each day. If one can silently recite it in the mind, with every single word penetrating back into the body, the effect is all the more wondrous. Doing this daily and observing it throughout life, then every request will naturally meet its response. A former worthy said: “The lower faculties should read it, the higher faculties should also read it; there is no one in the world who should not read it.” As for thoroughly cleansing and tidying the heart, this is the very first gate.
Encouraging Practice Is the Jewel of Obtaining Blessing

After reading the Tract of Response and Retribution, one must by all means accomplish deeds that accumulate virtue and amass merit. Those with wealth may emulate Judge Yang Xun of the prefecture, who recited the tract and constantly practiced ten great good deeds that benefit society. Through his accumulation of many good deeds Yang Xun had a son, Yang Chun, who at the age of twenty passed the examinations for the highest degree. Again, Mao Qizong of Rugao in Jiangsu during the Ming dynasty added annotations to the tract. His friend dreamed of an old man reciting it aloud and listened attentively. It was the two lines “Seeing another’s beauty, one gives rise to a thought of coveting it for oneself.” After the entire annotation was finished the old man said, “He should pass.” In the examination that year Mao Qizong in fact passed as a jinshi. This is an instance of doing good through the pen. Wang Yunzhi of Chengdu had a gift for speech, and Great Master Tongyuan taught him to accumulate virtue of the mouth. From then on, whenever there was a matter that benefited others, whether great or small, he spoke in its favor with all his might, never letting an opportunity slip. Having done this for twenty years, he passed the examinations again and again, and his two sons successively passed the examinations as well. This is an instance of doing good through the tongue.

Additionally, Cao Shimei of Shuntian, though his family was poor, rejoiced in doing good and sincerely urged and helped others. Others put out the money while he himself provided the labor. After many years, seeing that he could be trusted, they recommended him to a wealthy oil merchant to earn a share of the profits together. Thus he gradually gained a profit of more than five thousand taels of gold, and his descendants were able to enjoy deep blessing in peace. This is an instance of doing good through strength. From this one can see that Yang Xun’s ten good deeds may be learned by those who have wealth; and Mao Qizong’s pen, Wang Yunzhi’s tongue, and Cao Shimei’s strength may be learned by those without wealth. And reciting the tract is in essence none other than carrying on Heaven’s work of transformation. As for every movement and every stillness, always holding reverence in the heart so as to cultivate one’s own person — this is the same for rich and poor alike.
Encouraging Printing Is the Broadness of Obtaining Blessing

The Immortal Lord Taiwei’s Ledger of Merit and Demerit says: “To transmit a good book to one person is ten merits; to transmit it to ten people is a hundred merits. To transmit it to a great hero or great noble is a thousand merits; to spread it boundlessly and reprint it so that it never perishes is ten thousand merits.” Moreover, the Tract of Response and Retribution is especially a treasured instruction of salvation revered equally by heaven and man. From of old, whoever printed this scripture was sure to receive a remarkable recompense. For example, Huang Feng of Ruian printed this book, and after his life was ended the netherworld office released him and added to his years. Cheng Jiayou of Taigu printed this scripture; his allotted life had run out, but the great Bodhisattva caused him to be born again. Yao Wenran of Longshan printed this scripture and his malaria at once healed. The wife of Yu Yubi of Qiantang, née Liang, printed this scripture, and a critical illness of three years was suddenly cured in a single morning. These are instances of prolonging life and curing illness through efficacy.

Zhen Dakui printed this scripture and thereby had a son, gaining an heir. Wu Dazuo of Huizhou printed this scripture and successively had three sons. Wang Zhu of Xianju printed this scripture and his dead son was again reborn as his son. Gui Dabin printed this scripture and had a noble son. These are instances of gaining children where children were hard to obtain. There are also many instances of printing this scripture and gaining wealth, rank, and blessing. For example, Shen Ye of Huating passed the examinations because of it, and Yang Chen of Huangyan passed as jinshi. Shi Zhongpu of Jiangxi thus saw his family fortunes suddenly rise, and Fang Shike of Xiuning thus gradually prospered. As for those who printed this scripture and escaped flood — there was Xu Yunqing of Huizhou; those who escaped fire — there were Yang Zhenzhi of Wulin and Xu Tianxing of Jianggan. As for those who dreamed that Lord Guan the Emperor ordered them to print it — there was Li Susheng of Ningbo; those who dreamed that the Emperor Wenchang ordered them to print it — there was Lü Lüzhong. And still more, those who, praying for their parents’ blessing and longevity, had their wishes fulfilled — there was the filial son Wang Yuan of Qiantang.

Now I urge men of the world who read and recite the Tract of Response and Retribution to make a vow before the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, or spirits to print and distribute this scripture so that everyone in the world may read it. Whether a small volume or a large edition, whether donated alone or raised by many, it does not matter; one must print and give away ten thousand copies before the vow is fulfilled, and distribute them widely in public places so they circulate everywhere. The merit is immeasurable.
Encouraging Lecturing Is the Depth of Obtaining Blessing

The Supreme Old Lord composed the Tract of Response and Retribution to deliver the myriad ages, like a compassionate ferry in the sea of suffering, or a good medicine in times of grave illness. And men’s lecturing upon this scripture has likewise long been established. For example, in former times Zhou Chi of Suining Prefecture read the tract every day and delighted in expounding it to others, so that all who heard turned toward good. One day he suddenly fell gravely ill and his breath ceased. He saw a netherworld official say to him: “Your life was originally recorded in the ledger of hunger, but because you so often lectured on the Tract of Response and Retribution, your life has been prolonged and you are now entered in the ledger of longevity.” The official also said: “If one region upholds this scripture, that region is spared calamity; if the whole world upholds it, the whole world is peaceful and well-governed.” After Zhou Chi woke, he recorded the netherworld official’s words to admonish the world. Today the good men and women who read and recite the Tract of Response and Retribution should find time to lecture on this scripture for others, so that neighbors and villages may hear it constantly and be transformed into a place of benevolence — such hidden virtue is inconceivable.

The good people of today ought to set their hearts on urging others to do good, and must never merely cultivate only themselves. Teachers, in particular, should set aside a little time outside class to explain to their students the fundamental principles of being a good person. Students from primary school to university should all be taught these things, and they should also be urged to recite the Tract of Response and Retribution once each morning and observe it throughout their lives —
as an aid in cultivating their persons and establishing their undertakings. This is the hidden merit and accumulated virtue of a teacher.

Today, fathers and elder brothers who wish their children and younger brothers to be wise and good, to protect their families and attain wealth and honor, should often explain to them the principles and the proof-cases recorded in the Collected Expositions of the Tract of Response and Retribution, so that every son and grandson may love goodness and accumulate virtue. This is to create a blessing that flows far and long.

And after reading the Tract of Response and Retribution oneself, one should urge others to read it as well; after lecturing on it oneself, one should urge others to lecture on it as well. In lecturing, one must by all means speak again and again, freely and thoroughly, without tiring of detail, with utmost sincerity and earnestness; only then can one make those who hear leap up to reform their faults and move toward good, truly reaping the practical effect of the teaching.

Whether at home or in the monastery, one must revere those above and be harmonious with those below; endure what others cannot endure; do what others cannot do; take on others’ burdens as one’s own; help fulfill others’ good aims. In quiet sitting always reflect on one’s own faults; in idle conversation never discuss others’ failings. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying; in dressing and eating; from morning to night and from night to morning — one single recitation of the Buddha’s name, never let it be interrupted. Whether one recites in a low voice or silently, apart from reciting the Buddha’s name, give rise to no other thought. If a deluded thought should arise, at once cause it to be extinguished. Always give rise to a mind of shame and a mind of repentance. Even possessing attainment, always feel that one’s own effort is shallow; never boast or praise oneself. Manage only oneself and not others. Look only at good examples and not at bad ones. Regard all people as bodhisattvas, and consider only oneself to be truly an ordinary person. If one truly cultivates according to what I have said, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Shun all evil; practice all good; purify one’s own mind. This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha!
